title: Accounting standards, leases, and inventory
objectives: Answer out loud: How do leases affect EBITDA under each standard?
Answer out loud: LIFO vs. FIFO in inflation?

steps.body: US companies use US GAAP; most of the rest of the world uses IFRS. The differences matter when comparing international comps.
Under US GAAP (ASC 842), operating leases go on the balance sheet as a right-of-use asset and lease liability, but the expense stays as one straight-line operating cost — EBITDA unchanged.
Under IFRS 16, nearly all leases are treated like finance leases: expense splits into depreciation + interest, both *below* EBITDA. So EBITDA is higher for IFRS companies.
Inventory methods (FIFO, LIFO) change COGS and taxes when prices move.

blocks.title: Why do leases matter for EV/EBITDA?
blocks.body:
Consistency. If EBITDA excludes lease costs (IFRS), the lease liability must be in EV. If EBITDA includes lease costs (US GAAP operating leases), leave lease liabilities out of EV. Comparing a US retailer to a European one without adjusting can mislead by a full turn of EBITDA or more.

**Interview answer:** "Under IFRS, lease costs sit below EBITDA, so you'd add lease liabilities to EV. Under US GAAP they're in EBITDA, so you don't. Mixing them breaks comparability."

blocks.prompt: A European retailer reports under IFRS 16. To keep EV/EBITDA consistent, what should you do with its lease liabilities?

options.text: Leave them out of EV, since leases are operating items
Add them to EV, since IFRS EBITDA excludes lease costs

blocks.explanation: Under IFRS 16, lease costs sit below EBITDA (depreciation + interest), so the lease liability belongs in EV to match.

blocks.title: What's EBITDAR?
blocks.body: EBITDA before rent. It strips out lease costs so you can compare companies that own their real estate against those that lease. Pair it with EV including capitalized leases.

blocks.title: LIFO vs. FIFO — what changes when prices are rising?
blocks.teaser: FIFO sells the oldest (cheapest) inventory first → lower COGS, higher profit, higher taxes, and inventory on the BS closer to current cost.
blocks.body:
FIFO sells the oldest (cheapest) inventory first → lower COGS, higher profit, higher taxes, and inventory on the BS closer to current cost. LIFO sells the newest (most expensive) first → higher COGS, lower profit, lower taxes, more cash. IFRS bans LIFO.

**Interview answer:** "With rising prices, LIFO raises COGS and lowers taxes, so more cash. FIFO shows higher profit. IFRS doesn't allow LIFO."

blocks.title: Other IFRS differences worth knowing?
blocks.teaser: IFRS lets companies put interest paid and dividends paid in either operating or financing cash flow — so CFO can be inconsistent across companies.
blocks.body: IFRS lets companies put interest paid and dividends paid in either operating or financing cash flow — so CFO can be inconsistent across companies. IFRS also allows capitalizing some development costs that US GAAP expenses.
